utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everyone in around the courtroom. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is the case IT-04-75-T, The Prosecutor versus Goran Hadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. It's Matthew Olmsted and Elizabeth Spelman for the Prosecution, with Case Manager Thomas Laugel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic, for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. For the Defence of Goran Hadzic, Zoran Zivanovic and Christopher Gosnell with Corey Stevens, legal assistant, and Carlos Correa, legal intern.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. May the record show that Mr. Hadzic has waived his right to be present and has provided documentation to that effect. And may the record also reflect that the Trial Chamber is sitting 15 bis, Judge Mindua being absent. Today's hearing arises from the proprio motu order of the Trial Chamber issued on the 1st of April, 2015, ordering the appointment of independent experts to assist the Tribunal in the determination of Mr. Hadzic's -- whether Mr. Hadzic is fit to stand trial. The aim of this hearing is to have the appointed independent expert, Dr. Specenier, answer questions from the Prosecution, the Defence, and possibly the Chamber to provide further explanation and clarification regarding his expert report filed on 15 July 2015. The hearing will begin with 45 minutes of questioning from the Prosecution, followed by 45 minutes of questioning for the Defence and conclude with the Chamber's questions, if any. When hearing the expert, Dr. Martell, the parties opted for an open session with one particular restriction, however, at the request of the Defence. Unless the parties' position has changed, I would suggest the same course of action.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Our position has not been changed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No objection from the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So we will be in -- stay in open session. Could the Court Usher bring in the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Specenier. For the record, would you please state your name, your date of birth, and your profession.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My name is Pol Specenier. I am born on 21st -- 31st of January, 1955, and I'm a Belgian medical oncologist.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Next I will ask you to read the solemn declaration by which witnesses commit themselves to tell the truth and expose themselves to the penalty of perjury should they give false or untruthful information to the Tribunal. Please read out the solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Perhaps I should begin by asking you whether you prefer to be referred to as doctor or professor.

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Doctor is fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you. My name is Matthew Olmsted and I'm a Trial Attorney with the Prosecution, and I'm going to ask you a series of questions with regard to the report you prepared for this case. You brought a copy of that with you?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: I brought a copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Great. You conducted your examination of Mr. Hadzic on the 27th of June of this year; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And that examination consisted of both an interview as well as a physical examination?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I should just tell you now for -- I think we do have interpreters. We need to make sure there's a delay between my question and your response so they have time to --

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: -- to do their business. With regard to the physical examination, other than an unsure gait and a slight tremor, the results were normal. Is my understanding correct on that?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: I have -- I will check.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Objection. Objection, Mr. President. I don't know what is meant by the word "normal" and I'm not sure that the witness could understand what is meant by the word "normal".

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm referring to -- perhaps I should give the page number. Page 10, at the very bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Doctor, it's written, "Neurological examination was normal except for an unsure gait." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: That's correct. What I have to mention also is his performance status which was 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And I'll get to that in a moment, doctor. But just focussing right now on the results of your physician examination, you report that Mr. Hadzic's pulse rate at the start of the examination was 68 beats per minute and at the end was 80 beats per minute. That is within the range of the normal resting heart rate of an adult, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: As you just mentioned, you rated Mr. Hadzic's ECoG performance status as a two out of five, and if I'm correct, the ECoG performance status measures the level of a patient's autonomy in engaging in daily activities; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And according to the chart that you provide under footnote 6 of your report, an ECoG 2 means that Mr. Hadzic is capable of self-care and up and about for most of the day but unable to carry out any work; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Could you tell us what information did you base this ECoG assessment on.

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Well, it was based on his interview, on the questions about his activities and what was he -- what he was doing during the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So it was based upon his self-reporting to you?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Can you explain to us what is meant by "unable to carry out any work" under ECoG 2? What is meant by that term, "any work"?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: It's doing, well, any work, any activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Well, what kind of work did you have in mind when you made that assessment and --

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Working on the computer. Reading for a prolonged time, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And when you say "a prolonged time," how long would you mean?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: More than one hour, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Based on your own observations, is Mr. Hadzic capable of participating in a prolonged conversation and rationally and accurately answering your questions? I'm referring to page 11 of your report.

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: That's a difficult question. I think at this -- at that time, at that particular day, he was able to carry on a conversation with me for 80 minutes, at that particular time in that private situation, one on one, without interfering other persons. So this he was able to do. I think it's another matter to put him in a situation where many people are talking or when he is under stress because, of course, he was very relaxed. At that time in this situation, he was -- at that time he was able to have a conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I'll come back to the issue of him dealing with multiple people at the same time --

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: -- as you mention that later on in your report. Were you aware that as part of his neuropsychological examination which was conducted a couple of weeks after your examination, Mr. Hadzic responded to 567 questions, written questions, over approximately a three-hour period.

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: I have seen the report. I have the report with me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And would that qualify, responding to those 567 questions, would that qualify as work under ECoG?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Yes. This would qualify as work.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, going back to what you have said in your previous answer, I see that in your report at page 11 you caution that your interview with Mr. Hadzic is not entirely comparable to cross-examination or a situation where multiple people intervene, and you further caution that your interview had lasted for 80 minutes.

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I take it you made these cautionary remarks because they reflect your understanding of the activities that Mr. Hadzic might have to engage in during the course of his trial.

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: I had that in mind, yes, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Before you were contacted by this Tribunal, had you followed at all this case?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: During your interview with Mr. Hadzic, did he discuss with you any aspects of his case?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: No. He only very -- in a very vague way he said he had a responsibility or an activity at that time, but no particulars about the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I take it, then, you were not aware that Mr. Hadzic testified a year ago and therefore would not be subject to further cross-examination or examination --

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: -- in this case.

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you aware that Mr. Hadzic is represented in court by a legal team, including two Defence counsel, and therefore he is not directly involved in examining witnesses or making oral arguments or making written submissions in this case?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Were you aware that the Trial Chamber is considering proposals to complete this trial on an expedited basis, to shorten the trial day, to increase the number and length of breaks to allow Mr. Hadzic adequate time to recuperate and rest?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of any particular manner of conducting a trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: You also weren't aware that one of the proposals is that Mr. Hadzic stays in Serbia and he can follow the case, if he wants to, on videolink.

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No. Would you agree that these considerations are relevant to assessing Mr. Hadzic's ability to function for purposes of this trial?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: These would be pertinent, but you have to know -- you -- I come back to the statement, on that particular day, I assume that his situation is fluctuating, it's not a stable condition. His condition is evolving from day to day. And it is -- it can be expected that it will worsen rapidly. So one day, one hour, is not representative of a whole period of life.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: I understand that. But my question was -- and I think you -- I believe you did answer that these considerations, whether he has to face cross-examination or whether he has to withstand long court sessions, these considerations are relevant to determine whether he can function?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: These make it a little easier, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: On page 8 of your report, you mention that the 12 May 2015 MRI scan showed that the lesion in the right temporal lobe of Mr. Hadzic's brain had grown and that a new lesion was seen in his corpus callosum; correct?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Any did the MRI show lesions affecting any other parts of Mr. Hadzic's brain at the time?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: It was increased edema with shifting of the midline which is making an impact on the whole functioning of the brain.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Was there any indication that the cancer had spread to the eloquent portions of Mr. Hadzic's brain?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Generally, what does that mean in terms of cognitive function?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: That the cognitive function will decline.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: But my question is the fact that the cancer was not in the eloquent portion, what does that mean, when it's absent from that portion of the brain?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Well, it is interfering with speech but not with cognitive function.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Not with cognitive function.

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Not with -- well, yes, it's not interfering with verbal communication but it can interfere with cognitive function.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And just to clarify because I think we're going back and forth on this. The eloquent portion of the brain deals with cognitive function; correct?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Perhaps you can explain to us what the eloquent portion deals with.

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: I understand that this is with verbal communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And what portion deals with executive function?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: The whole brain deals with executive function.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And which portions deal with memory?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Well, there are several parts in the brain which interfere with memory. There is no particular point.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Now, is it based on these MRI results that you arrived at the conclusion that Mr. Hadzic was a recurrent glioblastoma patient?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And in your report, at pages 11 and 12, you provide statistical data on the probability of survival of patients with recurrent glioblastoma based on two phase three clinical trials involving three cancer treating drugs. And I believe you also go into more detail in footnote 7 and 8 of your report.

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And these clinical trials used two clinical end-points - overall survival and progression-free survival; correct?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And both used as their beginning points the date of randomisation. Could you explain to us what the date of randomisation was for purposes of these trials?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Well, that is the time when the treatment was chosen. The patients entered in a trial and they were allocated to one -- to one of the two arms, and the time of choosing the treatment arm is the time point at which starts that curve.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Would the date of randomisation be before or after the patient was diagnosed with recurrent glioblastoma?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: This will be at the time of diagnosis of recurrence. Mr. Hadzic would correspond to, let's say, April, May.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: He was -- the MRI showed progression and therefore that could be the point of recurrence?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: It would be the point of recurrence -- at that time he could be randomized in one of these trials and let's say within one month he would start with a new treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we could go into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Turning to progression-free survival, which is the second end-point these studies used, it appears the end-points were either the patient's glioblastoma worsened or the patient died.

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: In other words, the end-point for these patients wasn't necessarily death for this study?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: No, it could be progression.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And if we could look --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Kindly pause between questions and answers. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Olmsted, we are going too fast for the interpreters. Please pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you for the reminder, Mr. President. I see it on the screen. If we could call up on the screen 65 ter 6818.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And, doctor, I went on to the Internet and pulled off this first study by Wick et al on the clinical trial we were discussing, and if we could turn to page 3 and zoom in on the table on the bottom left part of the page, we can see that while a significant number of patients experienced disease progression during the study, only 15 died. Is that a correct reading of this?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: I think that's not entirely -- that's not completely correct. The patient reaches an end-point at progression or he dies, but he -- it -- as soon as the end-point is reached, the patient is not in this end-point category anymore. So he will -- they probably have died also. But the end-point was progression.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So in this study let me make sure that I understood you correctly, the end-point for the vast majority of these patients was progression and a handful, the end-point for them was their death.

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: The first end-point was progression in most of them and the first end-point was death in the other. But the end-point progression, of course, does not preclude a second end-point, death, which comes a little later.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the death need not be as a result of the cancer. It could be from any cause.

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: It could be from any cause, but in this type of tumour, overall the vast majority will be due to the cancer.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: May the interpreters kindly ask the doctor to speak into the microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Did you hear that --

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I see I've been reminded, Your Honour. I will do my best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: No, it's for Dr. Specenier. Did you hear, Dr. Specenier, the interpreters ask that you speak into the microphone. The Court Usher could perhaps re-direct the microphone a little bit.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll see. Please proceed, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: If we can look or zoom in towards the abstract, the -- I think it's the third paragraph, the abstract. We see that, in fact, five patients died for reasons unrelated to the cancer itself, four because of adverse events, and one was drug-related.

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: That's correct, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. Doctor, could you tell us, can brain tumour progression be asymptomatic, in other words only detectable through MRI results or other medical tests?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: It can.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: So progression may not necessarily impact a patient's ability to function.

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Not immediately, not necessarily immediately.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Other than overall survival and progression-free survival, there are other types of end-points; correct?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: There is a timed progression and others such as that.

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: And the reason clinical trials use different types of end-points is that each has their limitations.

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: For example, one of the limitations of overall survival is that the end-point, it includes deaths unrelated to cancer.

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: One of the limitations of progression-free survival is that it may be subject to investigator bias.

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: That's correct. But most of the time this is dealt with to -- by sending the images to a third party who evaluates the images, and in the case -- well, you are correct in saying that survival, overall survival, other causes of death are also important. But in the case of glioblastoma, this is not a large portion. Let's say in breast cancer or other tumour types this can be a bigger fraction of the patients. But in glioblastoma, the overall or the vast majority will be due to the glioblastoma.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Given these limitations --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Let me repeat myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Given these limitations but also given the fact that individual patients have individual characteristics/attributes, the results of these types of clinical trials can only provide an approximation as to when a particular patient suffering from glioblastoma will progress or may die; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Well, the trials are statistics. This is not -- you cannot say a lot about an individual patient. Indeed, when you start with a hundred patients, these are the outcomes. But, of course, as you already mentioned earlier, there are about 10 or 15 per cent who live longer than 14 months. You never know before who will be in this 15 per cent. This is a game of chances.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Clinical trials are not crystal balls.

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: No, these are meant to be statistics. But I have to say that you can have some ideas, of course, because relapse after one year after the end of treatment is not -- has a better prognosis than progressing during treatment. So we have to also take into account the characteristics of the disease. Mr. Hadzic had a progression just at the end of adjuvant treatment which is worse than when he would progress, let's say, after an interval of a year or longer. So these are also characteristics which you have to take into account. You have also to take into account that the tumour was not resected. It was only a biopsied. So these are all unfavorable characteristics of his disease. Another is that there was no MGMT methylation so it make the tumour less responsive to chemotherapy. So you have to balance all these characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Other characteristics --

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Can I say it other ways? Sorry for interrupting. It would surprise me very, very much if he would -- if he would be in the tail of the curve. I could be wrong, but it would surprise me.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Other characteristics that play into this would include the age of the patient --

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: -- as well as the location of the tumour --

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: -- and many other factors. In fact, I think I saw in one study that it could be as many as 50 to 60 factors, variables?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Gosnell, when you're ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Specenier. Am I pronouncing your name correctly?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Specenier.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Specenier. My name is Christopher Gosnell. I represent Mr. Hadzic, and I'll have a few questions for you today. If any of my questions, as they come from a layperson are not understandable or clear, please feel free to ask for clarification.

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: I'm a layperson in this setting also.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, at page 11 of your report, which I understand you have there in front of you, under the answer to question 2, you say, "The glioblastoma did not respond" - and you've underlined and bolded those words, "not respond" - "well to the treatment. In fact, the disease progressed," which means worsened, "despite the treatment. This assessment is based on the review of the MRI images performed at the MCH on May 12, 2015, which shows that the diameter of the largest lesion has increased, that there is a new lesion, and that there is edema with shift of the midline." And then back at page 8 of your report, you give a description as to how the visible lesion has increased in size, and you say that the lesion has increased from 2.9 by 2.6 centimetres, and I would understand that that was from the MRI in November --

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Base-line, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then that increased to 4.1 by 4.8 centimetres. So that means, if my math is more or less correct, it increased from 7.5 square centimetres to 20 square centimetres in size; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: That's correct. But -- well, that's correct. So we don't calculate in squares normally because, of course, a tumour is a sphere or an irregular volume.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: It's an irregular shape.

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: But would it be fair to say that it is approximately trebled in size?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: That's correct. At least.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And so that means now it's approximately - given it's an irregular shape - approximately, the circumference of a tennis ball.

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And regardless of the statistics about median progression, this itself constitutes progression, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: This is progression.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, in fact, that's -- I'm now using the word of one of the medical officers from the United Nations Detention Unit in her report of the 17th of June, in fact, that's dramatic progression, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: You can qualify it as dramatic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you say in your report, again back on page 11, that there is a new lesion. Can you tell us anything about the size of this new lesion?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Unfortunately, I did not measure it and I don't have the size with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can you give us an approximate relative to the size of the other lesion or --

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Small. I think less than a centimetre.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you say that there is a edema with shift of the midline. How large, how much in millimetres was the shift in the midline?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Again, I have to remind me on -- it would about 5 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And 5 millimetres, is that a significant shift?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: That's significant.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And is it right that when you have a shift of the midline of that degree we are talking about an indicator of significant intracranial pressure?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And intercranial pressure as reflected in that level of shift can be fatal, can it not?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: It can be fatal in a short -- relatively short-term.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: When you say "relatively short-term," do you mean to say that that can cause sudden death?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't expect sudden death. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what do you mean by short-term --

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: I would -- I would expect a gradual decline in his neurological functioning and in his consciousness. I would not expect a really sudden death.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Are we talking about symptoms that would manifest themselves week to week and lead to death?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: It can occur week to week, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, we'll have to go into private session for a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, Dr. Specenier, now I'd like to get away from mortality and we're not going to talk more about mortality. We're going to talk now about the deficits. And at page 12 of your report, you say:

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, can I just first ask: When you refer here to deficits, are you also referring to cognitive deficits?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you said earlier that after progression, you said the condition of a client can be expected to worsen rapidly. How rapidly? Are we talking one week to the next there can be a decline in --

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: There can be a deterioration one week to another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I am aware of the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And given the progress in the size of Mr. Hadzic's lesions -- lesion, the main lesion, that was observed between December and May, would you agree that it's quite possible - and we're talking now about his case - that he has worsened from week to week?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: It's very plausible, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that could have happened even during the two and a half weeks between your examination of Mr. Hadzic and the neuropsychologist's examination of Mr. Hadzic; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: That is completely right. And I think there are two differences between our examination. My examination was only an interview; his examination was very in-depth. These are -- is one explanation. Another potential explanation is I'm, like, which would also could -- it is very possible that in this interval, there was a decline in condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You performed no formal cognitive tests on Mr. Hadzic, did you?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You didn't perform any tests without the intercession of the interpreter; correct?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You didn't perform any tests in his own language?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: You didn't perform any non-verbal cognitive testing --

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- such as using diagrams or images?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And that's why, at page 11 of your report, you specifically say that a more thorough neuropsychological examination by a neuropsychologist is warranted; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And you'd agree with me, I guess, based on all those factors, that Dr. Martell is in a better position to give an opinion about his cognitive performance than you?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: I completely agree. And I also was aware of the fact that a more thorough examination was planned at the time I saw the patient, so I was aware that I did not have to do that because it was already scheduled.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If we can just refer again to this report from the medical officer dated the 8th of June, the end of paragraph 4, said: "With a new tumour treatment, this prognosis could possibly be extended with months." Now, Dr. Specenier, I won't mention the exact number of months because that's something that we're keeping out of the public eye, so I'm not going to mention the specific reference there. But then it says: "Of course, it cannot be predicted to what extent the treatment would be successful and to what side effects this would lead with the individual patient." And then paragraph 5 says: "And the DMO," that's the Deputy Medical Officer, "concluded in his report of the 22nd Mr. Hadzic decided not to go ahead with new chemotherapy in my professional opinion for obvious and understandable reasons." Now, can you think of any obvious and understandable reasons why he would not wish to continue with the particular course of chemotherapy that was proposed?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: The most obvious reason is, I think, the low chances of improving his prognosis. Because I think here the statement by Dr. Taphoorn are a little optimistic, because I think there are no real data that show that a second-line treatment really improves the survival. Therefore, I added this two publications showing that, in fact, it is very difficult to find any treatment which even improves the prognosis with a few weeks. That's -- and even -- not even -- and there's not many months. I think treatment does not make any difference, or very minimal difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And given Mr. Hadzic's reaction to the adjuvant chemotherapy, would there also be a danger of, in his case, a particular susceptibility of the side effects of the second-line chemotherapy --

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Sure --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- treatment?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Well, if I would be in his case, diagnosed with a recurrent disease, I would not accept second-line treatment for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Doctor, I just want to show you one last report with the assistance of the Registry. Doctor, I just would like you to direct your attention to paragraph 3 of this medical report, which is dated the 18th of June, 2015 from the Deputy Medical Officer. And he also is recording a communication with Professor Taphoorn, and he says: "I asked Professor Taphoorn whether a weekly telephone conversation with the Reporting Medical Officer would be too strenuous for Mr. Hadzic. He felt this was not the case. However, he did feel that cognitive testing would be too strenuous for Mr. Hadzic at this stage of his disease. Also, from a medical point of view, he felt this was not indicated." Now all I want to focus on for the -- as a preliminary is to understand the expression "at this stage of the disease," because you used that expression as well at page 12 of your report. In fact, it's the very last line of your report where you say: "However, it is not so that this choice will definitely have a negative impact on his survival as the benefit of treatment is minimal in that stage of this disease." What stage of disease are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: I am --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- for starters?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: -- referring to recurrent glioblastoma. Recurrent. That's the stage of his situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Does that encompass the notion of being post-progression?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And then Dr. Taphoorn says from a medical point of view, he felt this was not indicated. What does it mean in medical terminology when a doctor uses the expression that a particular course of action is "not indicated"?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: I suppose, but I'm not Dr. Taphoorn, of course, but I suppose he thinks that it -- that he would not do it. And I would not do it either.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Why would you not do it either?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Well, as I mentioned, his ECoG stage was 2, and I think I saw that he was -- he had to perform for more than two hours, which is long, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would you say that would pose a significant strain on him?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: It is a strain, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Would it be medically unhelpful?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: It will not improve his condition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: If he was required to do that day in, day out, would it damage his health?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: I think it could damage, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Those are my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Dr. Specenier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Dr. Specenier, this hearing comes to an end -- Yes, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. President. I didn't realise that there would be no questions from the Trial Chamber. May I just raise a few questions arising out of Defence counsel's examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Further Examination by Mr. Olmsted:

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: First of all, just with regard to the last line of questioning, I know you cannot interpret Dr. Taphoorn's words, but "could not indicated" also mean not necessary?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: It could.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, in your report, you found no signs of impaired memory, either long or short; correct?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Over your 25 years of experience as an oncologist, you've had -- had the opportunity to observe quite a number of cancer patients; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to object. I don't hear anything related to anything I asked Dr. Specenier about.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: It's coming, Your Honours, if I may. I was laying some foundation here. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, based on your 25 years of experience as an oncologist, what signs would you expect to find in a patient with a significantly impaired short-term memory?

utterances.speaker: POL SPECENIER
utterances.text: I wouldn't --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, I do object. This doesn't at all come out of any questions that I asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Objection sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, let me ask this, and this is with regard to the line of questioning regarding the interval between the doctor's examination of Mr. Hadzic and the examination conducted by Dr. Martell and that this is a variable situation and he may or may not have diminished in his cognitive abilities between those two points in time. My question is: Based upon your professional experience, would you expect signs of short-term memory loss to be noticeable in a patient whose short-term memory functions at the bottom 1 per cent of the population, based on your experience?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No, Mr. President, objection. Again, I'm sorry, but this is going -- this has nothing to do with the questions that were asked and the manner in which it was posed, I would suggest, is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. Olmsted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OLMSTED
utterances.text: All right. No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: So, Dr. Specenier, this is the end of the hearing. We thank you for coming to the Tribunal to assist us. You are released as a witness. The Court Usher will escort you out of the courtroom, and we wish you a safe journey home on this Friday evening with lots of traffic between The Hague and Antwerp.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The parties are aware of the fact that their submissions are expected to come in by Tuesday, if I'm not wrong? Then, if there is nothing else, court adjourned.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.35 p.m.,
